:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Consider the transformation $\mathbf{T}:(u,v,w) \to (x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)).$ The inverse transformation $\mathbf T^{-1}(x,y,z)\to(u(x,y,z), v(x,y,z), w(x,y,z))$ is given by
![](images/f8/f82cf760dee34626c290e29420fbaddb4ef254180087d05bb6fb883f2dc32e75.svg)

Find the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T.$

*Hint: You can assume that $x>0$, $y \ne 0.$*
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
For a transformation 

![](images/1c/1c2567cd1c2cf28ed17b6dc445025cb60061dc7d7d6c78c960be77f8866ef4a7.svg)

the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T,$ denoted $\dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (u, v, w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given $\mathbf T^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\dfrac{\partial (u, v, w)}{\partial (x, y, z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T$ using the relation

$$
\dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (u, v, w)} = \left( \dfrac{\partial (u, v, w)}{\partial (x, y, z)} \right)^{-1}.
$$

Here, we have 

$$
u(x,y,z) = x^2, \qquad 
v(x,y,z) = xy, \qquad
w(x,y,z) = yz.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =2x & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =y & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =x & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =z & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =y\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf{T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2x & 0 & 0 \\ y & x & 0 \\ 0 & z & y\end{aligned}| \\  & =2x|\begin{aligned}x & 0 \\ z & y\end{aligned}| \\  & =2x(xy-0) \\  & =2{x}^{2}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing down $\dfrac{\partial (u, v, w)}{\partial (x, y, z)}$ in terms of $u,$ $v,$ and $w,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}y & =2\cdot x\cdot (xy) \\  & =2\cdot \sqrt{u}\cdot v \\  & =2v\sqrt{u}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2v\sqrt{u}}.\end{aligned}
$$

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Finding the Jacobian of an Inverse Transformation

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Find the locations of all of the critical points of the transformation $\mathbf{T},$ where $\mathbf T$ is defined as

![](images/22/22690753019e406703952ae0c2a79450764b5ff42c758a03b2875a9d428d9e78.svg)
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
For a transformation 

![](images/be/be4c52a967cf6430f1d365ebb9b3a3a20bc852ac6422ed51e01dc5b39055c816.svg)

the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T,$ denoted $\dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (u, v, w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have 

$$
x(u,v,w) =w-u^3, \qquad 
y(u,v,w) = 2uv, \qquad
z(u,v,w) = u^2+v.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =-3{u}^{2} & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =1 \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =2v & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =2u & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =2u & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =1 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}-3{u}^{2} & 0 & 1 \\ 2v & 2u & 0 \\ 2u & 1 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =-3{u}^{2}|\begin{aligned}2u & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}|+1|\begin{aligned}2v & 2u \\ 2u & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-3{u}^{2}(0-0)+1(2v-4{u}^{2}) \\  & =2(v-2{u}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

The function has critical points when $\dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (u, v, w)} =0.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =0 \\ 2(v-2{u}^{2}) & =0 \\ v-2{u}^{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The equation $v-2u^2 = 0$ defines the parabolic cylinder $v=2u^2.$

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Determining the Critical Points of a Transformation

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Similar to transformations in the plane, we can also consider transformations of three-dimensional regions.

For example, the transformation

![](images/71/71b4c6b8f2db4890436050206115b94eb57b088be76049cb32667f02986b4f56.svg) 

maps a rectangular prism in Cartesian $uvw$-space onto one-eighth of a sphere in Cartesian $xyz$-space, as shown below.

![](images/3e/3e1ee5a6116d57cc1c3419b55bf0a9701b9f5d4d93931d053ed4a05b83a5d8f0.png)

 

In general, if a transformation

![](images/d1/d175f9eba3a6da7cc7750b3e59fe0e5904df27511a6b64481598e0f0ebfa1f0c.svg) 

is a $C^1$ transformation, meaning that it and its first derivatives are continuous, then the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf{T}$ is defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

  

For example, to compute the Jacobian determinant of our transformation above, we first calculate the required partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =-u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & =u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡v & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =-u\operatorname{sin}⁡v & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w & u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w & -u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w & u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w & u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡v & -u\operatorname{sin}⁡v & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡v|\begin{aligned}u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w & -u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w \\ u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w & u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w\end{aligned}|+u\operatorname{sin}⁡v|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w & -u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w & u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w\end{aligned}| \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡v\cdot {u}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡v\cdot ({cos}^{2}⁡w+{sin}^{2}⁡w)+u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\cdot u{sin}^{2}⁡v\cdot ({cos}^{2}⁡w+{sin}^{2}⁡w) \\  & ={u}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡v+{u}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡v \\  & ={u}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡v\cdot ({cos}^{2}⁡v+{sin}^{2}⁡v) \\  & ={u}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡v.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's get some practice at computing Jacobians of three-dimensional transformations.

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $\mathbf{T}$ that maps the Cartesian $uvw$-space onto the Cartesian $xyz$-space by means of the equations

$$
x = 2u-v,\qquad
y = u+3v+w,\qquad
z = u+2v-w.
$$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
For a transformation 

![](images/6e/6e94e780387ccbba3d8b6a6aaf5f00fbf362cd8163837a8ea78ad31c18f3b1b3.svg)

the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T,$ denoted $\dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (u, v, w)} ,$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =2 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =-1 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =1 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =3 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & =1 \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =1 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =2 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =2|\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}|-(-1)\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =2(-3-2)+(-1-1) \\  & =-10-2 \\  & =-12.\end{aligned}
$$

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Finding the Jacobian of a Three-Dimensional Transformation

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
The **critical points** of a transformation $\mathbf T: \mathbb R^3\longrightarrow\mathbb R^3,$ given by

![](images/0f/0f47dfd79a5147b5628975b26ea21a37288d809fb30a5a90b205ecc7b25ae008.svg)

are the points in Cartesian $uvw$-space where the Jacobian is zero:

$$
\dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (u, v, w)}=0
$$

  

Similar to the two-dimensional case, the transformation $\mathbf T$ is locally non-invertible at the critical points.

Finally, provided that $\mathbf{T}$ is invertible, the connection between the Jacobians of $\mathbf T$ and $\mathbf{T}^{-1}$ is as follows:

$$
\dfrac{\partial (u, v, w)}{\partial (x, y, z)} = \left( \dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (u, v, w)} \right)^{-1}
$$
:step/content.:tutorial/title: The Critical Points of a Transformation

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
The Jacobian determinant of a spatial transformation can be interpreted similarly to the Jacobian of a plane transformation.

As before, the Jacobian describes *local* effects, not global ones. 

Given that $J(u_0,v_0,w_0)$ denotes the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf{T}$ evaluated at $(u_0, v_0, w_0),$ let's describe $\mathbf T$'s effect on a *tiny* rectangular prism in Cartesian $uvw$-space whose bottom, back left corner is at the point $(u_0,v_0,w_0).$

![](images/31/31c0a7275acdac0dc217e73f3c1e3d9efe504832419c87486cee980e20ea04da.png)

 

It can be shown that, provided that our prism is very small and $(u_0,v_0, w_0)$ is not a critical point of $\mathbf T,$ the image of our prism can be approximated by a parallelepiped. 

The Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T$ evaluated at $(u_0,v_0,w_0)$ describes the following key features between our tiny rectangular prism and its (approximate) image:

- The local *volume* scale factor of $\mathbf T$. 

Suppose the length, width, and height of our rectangular prism are $\delta u,$ $\delta v,$ and $\delta w,$ so its volume is 

$$
\delta V = \delta u \delta v \delta w.
$$

 Then, it can be shown that the approximate parallelepiped in $xyz$-space has a volume equal to 

$$
\left|J(u_0,v_0,w_0)\right| \cdot \delta V,
$$

 as depicted below.

![](images/d6/d669cd5369d33e618ab43cfd3e93ee70c9fea8420b5a829d78826c11524511aa.png)

- Whether the transformation is *locally* orientation-preserving or *locally* orientation-reversing.

If $J(u_0,v_0,w_0) > 0,$ the transformation is (locally) orientation-preserving. 

Geometrically, this means that the transformation maps a triple of vectors onto a triple with the same orientation (right-handed $\to$ right-handed or left-handed $\to$ left-handed).

![](images/f0/f05f9a79d9156518e948c46f6c67eb5ff31132fd4a088e14219eada7eb49a441.png)

 

If $J(u_0,v_0, w_0) < 0,$ the transformation is (locally) orientation-reversing.

Geometrically, this means that the transformation maps a triple of vectors onto a triple with the opposite orientation (right-handed $\to$ left-handed or left-handed $\to$ right-handed).

![](images/45/45b08e0fec7114db52a05cb42ed46d7d62baa5b01a5dea37752928348802b205.png)

- Whether the transformation is *locally* invertible or *locally* non-invertible.

If $J(u_0,v_0,w_0) \neq 0,$ the transformation is (locally) invertible.

Geometrically, this means that the transformation maps our tiny rectangular prism (a three-dimensional region) onto a three-dimensional region (i.e., a parallelepiped).

![](images/61/61557eb2d78d468946375b918ab182da518b7cf2c68a1c0a0593c93b991bcf78.png)

 

If $J(u_0,v_0,w_0)= 0,$ the transformation is (locally) non-invertible.

Geometrically, this means that the transformation maps our tiny rectangular prism (a three-dimensional region) onto a two-dimensional region (a parallelogram), a one-dimensional region (a line segment), or a zero-dimensional region (a point).

![](images/72/726ba518de982ddd0b2924a645463b496ed881ead76a652c812c7a164aa684b8.png)
